clinicalPearls: Paroxysmal involuntary sustained contraction of one or more extraocular muscles causing episodic diplopia
Classically follows sellar or parasellar radiotherapy, often months to years later
Any of the ocular motor nerves may be affected, producing a transient strabismus in the field of the involved muscle
Attacks are often triggered by sustained eccentric gaze and last seconds to minutes
Between attacks ocular alignment may be normal, which can lead to misdiagnosis
Membrane-stabilising agents that reduce neuronal excitability are the usual treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Ocular neuromyotonia is attributed to impaired membrane stability and spontaneous or triggered discharges within an ocular motor nerve, frequently after radiation-induced or compressive injury that alters axonal excitability. The abnormal firing produces sustained contraction (tonic spasm) of the muscles supplied by the affected nerve, generating an intermittent deviation and diplopia, particularly after maintained eccentric gaze.
additionalInvestigations: Detailed history of prior cranial radiotherapy or sellar disease
MRI of the brain, orbits and cavernous sinus to exclude compression or recurrence
Orthoptic assessment during and between attacks
Acetylcholine-receptor antibody testing to exclude myasthenia when relevant
redFlags: New or progressive structural lesion on imaging
Signs of tumour recurrence in a previously irradiated field
Features suggesting myasthenia (fatigability, ptosis, bulbar signs)
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign for vision and often responds well to membrane-stabilising therapy, though symptoms can persist for years and may recur if treatment is stopped.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because alignment is normal between attacks
Attributing episodic diplopia to myasthenia without antibody or imaging workup
Overlooking a history of prior radiotherapy
Confusing sustained deviation with the shimmering oscillopsia of superior oblique myokymia
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Membrane-stabilising anticonvulsant therapy, typically carbamazepine, to suppress the paroxysmal extraocular muscle spasms
Symptomatic relief of diplopia between attacks with prisms or temporary occlusion where needed
Neuroimaging to exclude compression or recurrence of an underlying sellar or parasellar lesion, particularly after prior radiotherapy
Ongoing neuro-ophthalmology and orthoptic follow-up, with cautious continuation of therapy since symptoms may recur if treatment is stopped
Multidisciplinary input from neurology, ophthalmology and, where relevant, oncology
